l: trespass against a neighbor, Leviticus, Chapter 6
s: Such a trespass is also a trespass against the LORD, and includes dealing falsely in a deposit, bargain, or robbery, oppressing a neighbor, or lying and swearing falsely about a lost thing found. It requires full restitution plus a fifth and a trespass offering.

The offender who is found guilty must restore what he took, add a fifth part, and return it to its owner on the day he is found guilty. He then brings a ram without defect to the priest as a trespass offering and is forgiven after the priest makes atonement.

Restitution requires the guilty person to restore robbed goods, things gained by oppression, a deposit, a found lost thing, or anything sworn falsely about, in full. He must add a fifth part and give it to the owner on the day he is found guilty.

The trespass offering is a ram without defect from the flock, valued by estimation and brought to the priest. Through it the priest makes atonement before the LORD and the offender is forgiven. It is also named as most holy, along with the sin offering.

The burnt offering stays on the hearth on the altar all night until morning, and it is laid in order on the altar fire each morning. The sin offering is to be killed in the place where the burnt offering is killed.

The meal offering is presented by the sons of Aaron before the altar, where a handful of fine flour, oil, and all the frankincense is burned as a memorial portion for a pleasant aroma. The rest is eaten unleavened by Aaron and his sons in a holy place, and it is most holy. The priest's own meal offering, however, is made with oil on a griddle and wholly burned.

The sin offering is killed before the LORD where the burnt offering is killed, and it is most holy. The offering priest and every male priest eat it in the court of the Tent of Meeting, and whatever touches its flesh becomes holy. Garments splashed with its blood must be washed in a holy place, an earthen vessel used to boil it must be broken, and a bronze one scoured and rinsed. If its blood is brought into the Tent of Meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place, it must be burned with fire instead of eaten.

The altar holds the burnt offering on its hearth all night, and the priest removes ashes from it and sets them beside it. The handful of the meal offering is burned there, and the meal offering is presented before it.

The fire on the altar must be kept burning continually and must not go out. The priest burns wood on it every morning, lays the burnt offering in order on it, and burns the fat of the peace offerings on it.

Leviticus 7 gives the law of the trespass offering: it is most holy, is killed where the burnt offering is killed, has its blood sprinkled on the altar and its fat burned, and may be eaten by male priests in a holy place. It sets out which offerings belong to the priests, including the skin of the burnt offering and meal offerings, and gives rules for the peace offerings, including thanksgiving, vow and free will offerings, time limits on eating the meat, and the penalty of being cut off for eating it while unclean. The LORD speaks to Moses twice more, forbidding the children of Israel to eat fat of bull, sheep or goat and forbidding any blood, on penalty of being cut off. He also assigns the wave breast and heave right thigh of the peace offerings to Aaron and his sons as a portion forever. The chapter closes by summarizing the laws of the burnt, meal, sin, trespass, consecration and peace offerings, commanded at Mount Sinai.

The LORD speaks to Moses three times, giving the law of the offerings, forbidding the eating of fat and blood, and assigning priestly portions. He declares that he has taken the waved breast and heaved thigh from Israel's peace offerings and given them to Aaron and his sons forever. He commanded these laws at Mount Sinai.

Moses receives the LORD's words twice, with instructions to speak to the children of Israel about fat, blood, and the peace offering portions. The chapter ends noting that the LORD commanded him these laws at Mount Sinai.

Aaron and his sons are given the breast of the peace offerings as their consecrated portion forever. The text calls this portion the consecrated portion of Aaron, given on the day he and his sons were presented to minister in the priest's office.

The sons of Aaron share in every meal offering, whether mixed with oil or dry, one as well as another. They receive the waved breast, and the one among them who offers the blood and fat of the peace offerings receives the right thigh. Their portion is forever throughout their generations.

Every male among the priests may eat the trespass offering in a holy place. The priest who makes atonement keeps the sin and trespass offerings, and the priest who offers a burnt offering keeps its skin. The priest who offers a baked, pan or griddle meal offering keeps it, and the priest who sprinkles the blood of the peace offerings receives the heave offering portion. The priest burns the fat on the altar.

The children of Israel are told not to eat the fat of bull, sheep or goat, and not to eat any blood of bird or animal in any dwelling, on penalty of being cut off. They are to bring their peace offerings with their own hands, and give the breast and right thigh to the priests as a portion forever.

The trespass offering is most holy and is killed in the place of the burnt offering, with its blood sprinkled around the altar. Its fat, kidneys and liver cover are burned by the priest as an offering made by fire, and male priests eat the rest in a holy place. It has one law with the sin offering, and the priest who makes atonement with it has it.

The peace offerings have rules by type: a thanksgiving offering is accompanied by cakes and wafers and eaten on the day it is offered, while a vow or free will offering may be eaten that day and the next. Meat left until the third day is burned, and eating it then is not accepted and brings iniquity. Meat touching an unclean thing must be burned, and anyone eating it while unclean is cut off from his people. The priests receive the breast and right thigh.

The fat of the trespass offering, including the fat tail and the fat covering the innards, is burned on the altar by the priest. The children of Israel are forbidden to eat the fat of bull, sheep or goat. The fat of an animal that died of itself or was torn may be used for other service but never eaten, and eating the fat of an offering made by fire brings being cut off.

The blood of the trespass offering is sprinkled around on the altar. The children of Israel may not eat any blood, of bird or animal, in any dwelling, and whoever eats it is cut off from his people. The priest who sprinkles the blood of the peace offerings receives a portion.

l: peace offerings (waved breast and heaved thigh), Leviticus, Chapter 7
s: The breast of the peace offerings is waved as a wave offering before the LORD and belongs to Aaron and his sons. The right thigh is given to the priest as a heave offering, specifically to the one who offers the blood and fat. The LORD declares these portions given to Aaron and his sons forever from the children of Israel.

The LORD commands Moses to gather Aaron, his sons, the garments, anointing oil, a sin offering bull, two rams, and a basket of unleavened bread, and to assemble the congregation at the door of the Tent of Meeting. Moses washes and clothes Aaron and his sons, anoints the tabernacle, the altar, its vessels, and Aaron, and then offers the bull of the sin offering, the ram of the burnt offering, and the ram of consecration. Blood from the ram of consecration is put on the right ear, right thumb, and right great toe of Aaron and his sons, and portions are waved before the LORD and burned on the altar. Moses sprinkles anointing oil and altar blood on Aaron, his sons, and their garments, and instructs them to eat the meat and bread at the door, burn the remainder, and stay there seven days so they do not die. Aaron and his sons do everything the LORD commanded through Moses.

Moses carries out the LORD's commands for the ordination: he assembles the congregation, washes and clothes Aaron and his sons, anoints the tabernacle, altar, and Aaron, and performs the offerings. He takes the breast of the ram of consecration as his own portion and instructs Aaron and his sons to eat, burn the remainder, and remain at the door for seven days.

The LORD commands Moses to gather Aaron, his sons, the garments, oil, bull, rams, and bread, and to assemble the congregation. Each step is repeatedly described as done 'as the LORD commanded Moses,' and the burnt and consecration offerings are called a pleasant aroma and an offering made by fire to him.

Aaron is washed, clothed with the tunic, sash, robe, ephod, breastplate with the Urim and Thummim, and turban with the golden plate, and anointed with oil on his head. He lays his hands on the offerings, receives blood on his right ear, thumb, and great toe, holds the wave offering, and is sanctified along with his garments.

Aaron's sons are washed and clothed with tunics, sashes, and headbands, and they lay their hands on the bull and both rams. They receive blood on their right ear, thumb, and great toe, hold the wave offering, are sprinkled with oil and blood, and are told to eat the consecration meal and stay at the Tent of Meeting seven days.
The congregation is assembled at the door of the Tent of Meeting at the LORD's command. Moses tells them that this is the thing the LORD has commanded to be done.

The door of the Tent of Meeting is the site where the congregation assembles and where the ordination takes place. Aaron and his sons must boil and eat the meat and bread there and must not leave for seven days, day and night.

Moses sprinkles anointing oil on the altar seven times and anoints it and its vessels, the basin, and its base to sanctify them. He purifies it with the bull's blood on its horns and at its base, sprinkles ram's blood around it, and burns the fat, the burnt offering ram, and the consecration offerings on it.

Moses uses the anointing oil to anoint and sanctify the tabernacle and all in it, the altar and its vessels, the basin and its base, and Aaron's head. He later sprinkles oil mixed with altar blood on Aaron, his sons, and their garments to sanctify them.

Aaron is clothed with the tunic, sash, robe, ephod with its skillfully woven band, breastplate holding the Urim and Thummim, turban, and golden plate, the holy crown. His sons receive tunics, sashes, and headbands, and the garments are sprinkled with oil and blood to sanctify them.

l: bull of the sin offering, Leviticus, Chapter 8
s: Aaron and his sons lay their hands on the bull's head, and it is killed. Its blood purifies and sanctifies the altar to make atonement for it, its fat, liver cover, and kidneys are burned on the altar, and the rest of the bull is burned outside the camp.

l: ram of the burnt offering, Leviticus, Chapter 8
s: Aaron and his sons lay their hands on this ram, which is killed, and its blood is sprinkled around the altar. It is cut into pieces, and after the innards and legs are washed, the whole ram is burned on the altar as a pleasant aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD.

After Aaron and his sons lay their hands on it and it is killed, its blood is put on the right ear, thumb, and great toe of Aaron and his sons and sprinkled around the altar. Its fat and right thigh, with bread from the basket, are waved and burned on the altar, the breast is Moses' portion, and the meat is to be boiled and eaten at the door.

l: ordination of Aaron and his sons, Leviticus, Chapter 8
s: The ordination is a ceremony of washing, clothing, anointing, and offerings carried out by Moses before the assembled congregation, ending with a seven-day stay at the Tent of Meeting door. Moses says it was done at the LORD's command to make atonement for them, and Aaron and his sons do all that was commanded.

On the eighth day Moses summons Aaron, his sons, and the elders of Israel and instructs them on the offerings to be made before the LORD, promising that the LORD will appear that day. Aaron offers a sin offering and burnt offering for himself, then the people's goat sin offering, burnt offering, meal offering, and peace offerings of a bull and a ram, with his sons delivering the blood and the fat being burned on the altar. Aaron waves the breasts and right thigh as a wave offering and blesses the people. Moses and Aaron enter the Tent of Meeting and come out to bless the people, and the LORD's glory appears to all. Fire comes out from before the LORD and consumes the burnt offering and fat on the altar, and the people shout and fall on their faces.

Moses calls Aaron, his sons, and the elders on the eighth day and commands the offerings the LORD requires, telling the people that the LORD's glory will appear. He directs Aaron to make atonement for himself and the people, then goes with Aaron into the Tent of Meeting and blesses the people when they come out.

Aaron carries out the offerings Moses commanded: he kills the calf of the sin offering for himself, then offers the people's goat, burnt offering, meal offering, and peace offerings, burning the fat on the altar and waving the breasts and right thigh. He lifts his hands to bless the people, enters the Tent of Meeting with Moses, and blesses the people again.

The children of Israel are told to bring a male goat, a calf and a lamb, a bull and a ram, and a meal offering mixed with oil, and the congregation brings these and stands before the LORD. They are blessed by Aaron and by Moses and Aaron, and when they see fire consume the offering on the altar, they shout and fall on their faces.

The LORD has commanded the offerings and the procedures Moses relays, and Moses says the LORD appears to the people that day. The LORD's glory appears to all the people, and fire comes out from before the LORD to consume the burnt offering and fat on the altar.

l: glory of the LORD, Leviticus, Chapter 9
s: Moses promises that the LORD's glory will appear to the people once they do what was commanded. After Moses and Aaron come out of the Tent of Meeting and bless the people, the LORD's glory appears to all the people.

l: Fire (from before the LORD), Leviticus, Chapter 9
s: Fire comes out from before the LORD and consumes the burnt offering and the fat upon the altar. Seeing it, all the people shout and fall on their faces.

Aaron draws near to the altar to make the offerings. He puts blood on its horns, pours blood at its base, sprinkles blood around it, and burns the fat, burnt offering pieces, and meal offering on it. Fire from before the LORD finally consumes the burnt offering and fat upon it.

Aaron offers a calf as a sin offering for himself and a goat as a sin offering for the people. For the calf, he puts blood on the altar's horns, burns the fat, kidneys, and liver cover on the altar, and burns the meat and skin outside the camp. The people's goat is offered in the same way as the first.

A ram for Aaron and a calf and lamb for the people are commanded as burnt offerings, and Aaron kills his burnt offering with his sons delivering the blood to sprinkle around the altar. He burns the pieces and head, the washed innards and legs, and offers the people's burnt offering according to the ordinance. Fire from the LORD later consumes the burnt offering on the altar.

A bull and a ram are commanded as the people's peace offerings, and Aaron kills them, with his sons delivering the blood to be sprinkled around the altar. The fat, fat tail, innard covering, kidneys, and liver cover are burned on the altar, and Aaron waves the breasts and right thigh as a wave offering before the LORD.

Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, offer strange fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded, and fire from before the LORD devours them. Moses tells Aaron that this fulfills the LORD's word about showing himself holy, and Aaron holds his peace. Moses has Mishael and Elzaphan carry the bodies out of the camp, and instructs Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar not to mourn openly or leave the Tent of Meeting. The LORD forbids Aaron and his sons wine and strong drink when entering the Tent of Meeting and commands them to distinguish holy from common and to teach the statutes. Moses directs the remaining sons to eat the meal offering and portions, then becomes angry that the sin offering goat was burned rather than eaten, until Aaron explains and Moses is satisfied.

Nadab, a son of Aaron, took his censer, put fire and incense in it, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which had not been commanded. He was devoured by fire from before the LORD and died, and his body was carried out of the camp in his tunic.

Abihu, a son of Aaron, took his censer with Nadab and offered strange fire before the LORD, which had not been commanded. He was devoured by fire from before the LORD and died, and his body was carried out of the camp in his tunic.

Aaron is told by Moses that the deaths of his sons fulfill what the LORD spoke about being shown holy, and he holds his peace. The LORD speaks to him directly, forbidding wine and strong drink for him and his sons when entering the Tent of Meeting and charging them to distinguish holy from common and teach the statutes. When Moses questions the burned sin offering, Aaron answers that such things have happened to him and asks whether eating it would have pleased the LORD, which satisfies Moses.

The LORD had not commanded the strange fire, and fire came from before him and devoured Nadab and Abihu. He spoke to Aaron, forbidding wine and strong drink for the priests when entering the Tent of Meeting as a perpetual statute, and commanding them to distinguish holy from common and unclean from clean and to teach his statutes. Moses cites his word that he will show himself holy to those who come near and be glorified before all the people.

Moses interprets the deaths as the fulfillment of the LORD's word, has Mishael and Elzaphan carry the bodies out, and instructs Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar not to mourn openly or leave the Tent of Meeting. He directs the remaining sons to eat the meal offering and the breast and thigh portions in a holy or clean place. He becomes angry on finding the sin offering goat burned, but is pleased by Aaron's reply.

Eleazar, a son of Aaron who survives, is told by Moses not to let his hair go loose or tear his clothes and not to leave the Tent of Meeting. He is told to eat the remaining meal offering beside the altar, and Moses is angry with him and Ithamar when the sin offering goat is found burned.

Ithamar, a son of Aaron who survives, is told by Moses not to let his hair go loose or tear his clothes and not to leave the Tent of Meeting. He is told to eat the remaining meal offering beside the altar, and Moses is angry with him and Eleazar when the sin offering goat is found burned.

l: strange fire (offered by Nadab and Abihu), Leviticus, Chapter 10
s: The strange fire was placed in censers with incense and offered before the LORD by Nadab and Abihu. The text says the LORD had not commanded it, and it precedes their death.

l: fire (from before the LORD), Leviticus, Chapter 10
s: Fire came out from before the LORD and devoured Nadab and Abihu, and they died before the LORD. Moses calls this burning one that the LORD has kindled, for which the whole house of Israel may mourn.

l: wine and strong drink prohibition, Leviticus, Chapter 10
s: The LORD commands Aaron and his sons not to drink wine or strong drink whenever they go into the Tent of Meeting, on penalty of death. It is a statute forever throughout their generations, tied to their duty to distinguish holy from common and clean from unclean and to teach Israel the statutes.

Moses diligently inquired about the goat of the sin offering and found it had been burned. He angrily said it should have been eaten in the sanctuary since it was most holy and its blood was not brought inside. Aaron's explanation pleased Moses.

l: death of Nadab and Abihu, Leviticus, Chapter 10
s: Nadab and Abihu died when fire from the LORD devoured them for offering strange fire. Their bodies were carried in their tunics out of the camp by Mishael and Elzaphan, and Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar were forbidden to mourn openly, while the rest of Israel could bewail the burning.

The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron, instructing them to tell the children of Israel which living things may and may not be eaten. Land animals must part the hoof, be cloven-footed, and chew the cud; the camel, hyrax, hare, and pig are named as unclean. Water creatures must have fins and scales, and a list of birds and most winged insects are forbidden, though locusts, katydids, crickets, and grasshoppers may be eaten. Touching or carrying carcasses of unclean animals, including creeping things such as the weasel, rat, and lizards, brings uncleanness until evening and sometimes washing of clothes, and vessels contaminated by them must be washed or broken. The chapter closes with the call to be holy because the LORD is holy, and a statement that these laws distinguish the unclean from the clean.

The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives the laws on which animals may be eaten. He declares that He is the LORD their God who brought Israel out of Egypt, commands them to sanctify themselves and be holy because He is holy.
Moses, together with Aaron, is addressed by the LORD and told to speak to the children of Israel about the living things they may eat. He serves as the one who relays the dietary laws.
Aaron is addressed by the LORD along with Moses as a recipient of the instructions on clean and unclean animals. The message to be passed on to Israel is given to both of them.

The children of Israel receive rules on which animals they may eat and which they must not eat or touch. They are told to avoid making themselves abominable or defiled and to be holy because the LORD, who brought them out of Egypt, is holy.

l: clean and unclean animals, Leviticus, Chapter 11
s: The chapter sets out the distinction between clean animals that may be eaten and unclean ones that may not. It concludes that the law exists to make a distinction between the unclean and the clean, and between the living thing that may be eaten and the one that may not.

l: land animals (Chapter 11 dietary rules), Leviticus, Chapter 11
s: Land animals may be eaten if they part the hoof, are cloven-footed, and chew the cud. The camel, hyrax, and hare chew the cud but lack a parted hoof, and the pig has a split hoof but does not chew the cud, so all four are unclean; their meat may not be eaten and their carcasses may not be touched. Animals that go on paws are also unclean.

Creatures in the seas and rivers that have fins and scales may be eaten. All others that move in the waters, lacking fins and scales, are an abomination: they are not to be eaten and their carcasses are to be detested.

A list of birds is declared an abomination and not to be eaten, including the eagle, vulture, black vulture, kites, ravens, owls, gull, hawk, cormorant, osprey, stork, heron, and hoopoe. The bat is also included in the list.

Flying insects that walk on all fours are an abomination, as are all winged creeping things with four feet. An exception is made for those with long, jointed legs for hopping, so locusts, katydids, crickets, and grasshoppers may be eaten.

Creeping things that creep on the earth are an abomination and are not to be eaten, whether they go on the belly, on all fours, or have many feet. The weasel, rat, great lizards, gecko, monitor lizard, wall lizard, skink, and chameleon are named as unclean, and touching them dead brings uncleanness until evening.

Touching or carrying the carcass of an unclean animal makes a person unclean until evening, and carriers must wash their clothes. Anything onto which such a carcass falls becomes unclean: vessels are put in water, earthen vessels, ovens, and ranges are broken, while springs, cisterns, and dry seed for sowing stay clean. Even the carcass of a normally edible animal that dies makes the one who touches, eats, or carries it unclean until evening.

Uncleanness is contracted by touching or carrying carcasses and lasts until evening, with washing of clothes required for carrying or eating them. Contaminated vessels used for work must be put into water and are clean again by evening, while earthen vessels and ovens must be broken. Food or drink that has been soaked in water or held in contaminated vessels becomes unclean.

The LORD commands Israel to sanctify themselves and be holy because He is holy. Avoiding defilement by creeping things and keeping the clean and unclean distinctions is presented as the way to be holy.

The LORD speaks to Moses, instructing him to tell the children of Israel the law for a woman who gives birth. After bearing a male child she is unclean seven days, the boy is circumcised on the eighth day, and she remains in the blood of purification thirty-three more days. After bearing a female child she is unclean two weeks and remains in the blood of purification sixty-six days. During this time she may not touch any holy thing or enter the sanctuary. When the days are completed she brings a year old lamb for a burnt offering and a young pigeon or turtledove for a sin offering to the priest at the door of the Tent of Meeting, who makes atonement so she is cleansed; if she cannot afford a lamb, she brings two turtledoves or two young pigeons instead.

The LORD speaks to Moses and gives the law concerning a woman who bears a child, setting out the periods of uncleanness and purification and the offerings required. The offerings are made before the LORD.

l: woman who bears a child, Leviticus, Chapter 12
s: After bearing a child she is unclean and may not touch any holy thing or enter the sanctuary until her days of purifying are completed. When they are over she brings offerings to the priest at the door of the Tent of Meeting, and atonement is made so that she is cleansed. If she cannot afford a lamb, she may bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons.

l: male child (born to the woman), Leviticus, Chapter 12
s: The male child is circumcised on the eighth day. His birth makes his mother unclean for seven days, followed by thirty-three days in the blood of purification.

l: female child (born to the woman), Leviticus, Chapter 12
s: The birth of a female child makes her mother unclean for two weeks, followed by sixty-six days in the blood of purification. The same offerings are required as for a son.

The priest receives the woman's offerings at the door of the Tent of Meeting and offers them before the LORD. He makes atonement for her, and she is then clean. If she brings two birds, he makes atonement for her in the same way.

A woman who bears a son is unclean seven days, as in her monthly period, and one who bears a daughter is unclean two weeks. The uncleanness is followed by a further period in the blood of purification during which she may not touch holy things or enter the sanctuary.

The blood of purification lasts thirty-three days after a son and sixty-six days after a daughter. When these days are completed, the woman brings her offerings, and the priest's atonement cleanses her from the fountain of her blood.

A year old lamb is to be brought as a burnt offering when the days of purification are completed. If the woman cannot afford a lamb, one of two turtledoves or young pigeons serves as the burnt offering.
A young pigeon or a turtledove is brought as the sin offering when the days of purification are completed. If the woman cannot afford a lamb, the second of her two birds is the sin offering.
A year old lamb is the prescribed burnt offering for the woman after her purification days. If she cannot afford one, two turtledoves or two young pigeons are allowed in its place.

l: turtledoves and young pigeons, Leviticus, Chapter 12
s: A young pigeon or a turtledove is the sin offering the woman brings with her lamb. If she cannot afford a lamb, she takes two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for the burnt offering and the other for the sin offering.

Chapter 13 records the LORD's instructions to Moses and Aaron on how skin diseases called leprosy are to be diagnosed. The priest examines swellings, scabs, bright spots, boils, burns, and plagues on the head or beard, looking at depth, white hair, and spread, and isolates the person for seven-day periods before pronouncing them clean or unclean. A person with leprosy must wear torn clothes, let their hair hang loose, cover the upper lip, cry 'Unclean!', and live alone outside the camp. The chapter then turns to mildew in garments of wool, linen, or leather, which the priest examines, isolates, and has washed, burning the item if the plague spreads or stays unchanged. It closes by calling this the law of the plague of mildew for pronouncing a garment clean or unclean.
The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives the laws for diagnosing leprosy in people and mildew in garments. Through these instructions he sets how the priest is to judge what is clean and unclean.

The priest examines each plague, judging its depth, the color of the hair, and whether it has spread, and he isolates the person or the item for seven days at a time. He pronounces the person or garment clean or unclean, and commands washing or burning of affected garments.

Leprosy is described through signs such as a swelling, scab, or bright spot deeper than the skin, white hair in the plague, and raw flesh. It can break out in a boil, a burn, or on the head or beard, and a dull white rash is not leprosy. If it covers all the flesh and has turned white, the person is clean, but raw flesh makes them unclean.

l: infected person (person with leprosy), Leviticus, Chapter 13
s: The infected person is brought to the priest, may be isolated for seven days or more, and is pronounced clean or unclean. One declared leprous must wear torn clothes, let the hair hang loose, cover the upper lip, cry 'Unclean! Unclean!', and dwell alone outside the camp. If cleared, the person washes their clothes and is clean.

Mildew, called a destructive mildew, is a greenish or reddish plague in wool, linen, or leather that is treated like leprosy. If it spreads or does not change color after washing, it is unclean and the item is burned, but if it fades the affected part is torn out.

A garment of wool, linen, or leather with a greenish or reddish plague is shown to the priest and isolated for seven days. If the plague spreads it is burned, but if it does not spread it is washed and isolated seven more days. If the plague departs after washing, the garment is washed a second time and is clean.

Leviticus 14 gives the LORD's instructions to Moses, and later to Moses and Aaron, on how a priest cleanses a person healed of leprosy. The ritual begins outside the camp with two living birds, cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop, followed by washing, shaving, a seven-day wait, and on the eighth day trespass, sin, burnt, and meal offerings, with blood and oil applied to the ear, thumb, and big toe. A poorer person may offer one lamb plus turtledoves or young pigeons in place of the full set of animals. The chapter then covers mildew in a house in Canaan, which the priest inspects, shuts up for seven days, and then scrapes, repairs, or tears down if it spreads, and cleanses with a bird ritual if it is healed. It closes by summarizing this as the law for leprosy, itch, mildew in garments and houses, swelling, scab, and bright spot, to teach what is clean and unclean.

The LORD speaks to Moses, and then to Moses and Aaron, giving the law for cleansing a healed leper and for dealing with mildew in houses. He says that he will put the spreading mildew in a house in the land of Canaan, which he gives to them as a possession.

The priest goes out of the camp to examine the leper, directs the two-bird ritual, sprinkles, and pronounces the person clean. On the eighth day he offers the sacrifices, puts blood and oil on the person's right ear, thumb, and big toe, and makes atonement. He also inspects the mildewed house, orders it emptied, shuts it up for seven days, directs the removal of stones and scraping, and pronounces it clean or orders it torn down.

l: infected person (person with leprosy), Leviticus, Chapter 14
s: The leper, once healed, is brought to the priest and is sprinkled seven times and pronounced clean. He washes his clothes, shaves all his hair, and bathes, then dwells outside his tent seven days before shaving and washing again on the seventh day. On the eighth day he brings offerings, receives blood and oil on his ear, thumb, and toe, and is made clean by atonement, with a poorer alternative allowed if he cannot afford the full offering.

Leprosy is treated as a plague that makes a person unclean until the priest examines him and finds it healed. The chapter's closing summary names it with itch, mildew of a garment or house, swelling, scab, and bright spot, as conditions the law teaches to distinguish as clean or unclean.

l: cleansing ritual for the leper (two birds), Leviticus, Chapter 14
s: The priest has two living clean birds, cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop brought. One bird is killed in an earthen vessel over running water, and the living bird, cedar, scarlet, and hyssop are dipped in its blood. The one to be cleansed is sprinkled seven times and pronounced clean, and the living bird is let go into the open field. The same bird ritual is used to cleanse a house that has been healed of mildew.

On the eighth day the person brings two male lambs, a ewe lamb, fine flour mixed with oil, and a log of oil. One male lamb is the trespass offering and is waved with the oil, and the sin offering, burnt offering, and meal offering follow to make atonement. A poor person brings one male lamb for the trespass offering, a smaller amount of flour and oil, and two turtledoves or young pigeons, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering.

A house in Canaan with a spreading mildew, shown by greenish or reddish hollow streaks deeper than the wall, is reported by its owner to the priest. The priest has it emptied, shuts it up seven days, and if the plague has spread has the infected stones removed and the house scraped and replastered. If the mildew returns, the house is destructive and unclean and is broken down, with its materials carried to an unclean place outside the city, but if it does not spread it is pronounced clean and cleansed with the bird ritual.

Leviticus 15 gives the LORD's instructions, spoken to Moses and Aaron for the children of Israel, on ritual uncleanness from bodily discharges. A man with a discharge makes unclean the beds, seats, saddles, and vessels he uses, and people who touch him or these things must wash their clothes, bathe, and remain unclean until evening. After he is cleansed he counts seven days, bathes in running water, and on the eighth day brings two turtledoves or young pigeons to the priest for a sin offering and a burnt offering. Emission of semen requires bathing and uncleanness until evening, and a woman's menstrual period or prolonged blood discharge brings seven days of impurity that spreads to what she lies on or sits on and to those who touch her. The chapter ends by stating that these laws separate Israel from their uncleanness so they do not die by defiling the tabernacle.

The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives the laws about discharges and uncleanness. He is the one before whom the priest makes atonement, and he has a tabernacle among the people that uncleanness would defile.
Moses is addressed by the LORD, together with Aaron, and is told to speak to the children of Israel about the laws of discharges.
Aaron is addressed together with Moses as the LORD begins giving the laws on discharges.

The children of Israel are given instructions on how to handle uncleanness from discharges, including washing, bathing, waiting, and offerings. The laws are meant to separate them from their uncleanness so they do not die when they defile the LORD's tabernacle among them.

l: man with a discharge, Leviticus, Chapter 15
s: A man with a discharge is unclean whether it is running or has stopped, and he makes unclean his bed, whatever he sits on, his saddle, and vessels he touches. Anyone who touches him or these things must wash and bathe and is unclean until evening. After being cleansed he counts seven days, bathes in running water, and on the eighth day brings two birds to the priest.

l: woman with a discharge, Leviticus, Chapter 15
s: A woman with a bloody discharge is impure seven days, and whatever she lies or sits on is unclean, as is anyone who touches her or those things. If her discharge continues beyond her period, she remains unclean for all those days, and once cleansed she counts seven days and on the eighth brings two birds to the priest.

The priest receives the two turtledoves or young pigeons at the door of the Tent of Meeting on the eighth day. He offers one as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering and makes atonement before the LORD for the man or woman.

Uncleanness is created by discharges and by emission of semen, and it spreads through touch, lying, or sitting to people and objects. It usually lasts until evening, but longer in some cases, such as seven days for a man who lies with a menstruating woman, and it can defile the tabernacle and bring death.

A bodily discharge, whether flowing or stopped, makes a man unclean, and a woman's blood discharge outside her period makes her unclean for its duration. Cleansing requires seven days of counting, washing, and bathing, followed by offerings on the eighth day.

An emission of semen requires the man to bathe all his flesh and be unclean until evening, and any garment or skin with semen on it must be washed and is unclean until evening. A man and woman who lie together with an emission must both bathe and are unclean until evening.

A woman's period brings seven days of impurity, during which what she lies or sits on is unclean and anyone touching her or those things is unclean until evening. A man who lies with her and gets her flow on him is unclean seven days, and a discharge beyond her period is treated like her period.

Washing clothes and bathing in water are required of those who touch an unclean person or object, and they stay unclean until evening. A person cleansed of a discharge must bathe in running water after the seven days, and garments with semen on them are washed.

l: sin offering and burnt offering, Leviticus, Chapter 15
s: On the eighth day after cleansing, a man or woman with a discharge brings two turtledoves or young pigeons to the priest, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering. The priest offers them to make atonement before the LORD for the discharge.

After the death of Aaron's two sons, the LORD tells Moses to warn Aaron not to enter the Most Holy Place at just any time, lest he die. Aaron is to enter only after bathing and putting on the holy linen garments, bringing a young bull for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering for himself, and taking two goats and a ram from the congregation of Israel. He kills the bull, brings incense and blood within the veil, and sprinkles blood on the mercy seat, then does the same with the blood of the people's sin offering goat, atoning for the Holy Place, the Tent of Meeting, and the altar. Aaron lays his hands on the live goat, confesses Israel's sins over it, and sends it into the wilderness by a man who is ready, with rules for washing and for burning the bull and goat outside the camp. The LORD establishes a permanent statute for the tenth day of the seventh month, a Sabbath of solemn rest and afflicting souls, when atonement is made once a year for all Israel's sins.

The LORD speaks to Moses after the death of Aaron's two sons and gives detailed instructions for when and how Aaron may enter the Most Holy Place. He says he will appear in the cloud on the mercy seat, and he establishes the yearly atonement as an everlasting statute for Israel.

Moses receives the LORD's instruction to tell his brother Aaron not to come at just any time into the Most Holy Place. At the end, it is said that the instructions were done as the LORD commanded Moses.

Aaron is told to enter the Most Holy Place only in the prescribed way: bathed, wearing the holy linen garments, and bringing a bull and a ram. He offers the bull for himself and his house, casts lots for the two goats, brings incense and blood within the veil, atones for the sanctuary and altar, confesses Israel's sins over the live goat, and then offers burnt offerings for himself and the people.

The children of Israel supply the two male goats and a ram for the offerings. Their uncleanness, transgressions, and sins are atoned for, and the iniquities are placed on the live goat that carries them away. They are commanded, along with natives and strangers among them, to afflict their souls and do no work on the tenth day of the seventh month.

The Most Holy Place lies within the veil, before the mercy seat on the ark, where the LORD appears in the cloud. Aaron may enter it only at the prescribed time and manner, with incense covering the mercy seat so that he will not die, and blood is sprinkled there on the mercy seat and before it.

The Tent of Meeting is where the two goats are set before the LORD at its door. It dwells with Israel in the middle of their uncleanness and receives atonement; no one may be in it while Aaron enters to make atonement, and he leaves the linen garments there afterward.

l: bull of the sin offering (Aaron's bull), Leviticus, Chapter 16
s: The young bull is the sin offering for Aaron himself and his house, and he kills it. Its blood is sprinkled on the mercy seat and seven times before it, and some is put on the altar's horns. Its skin, flesh, and dung are burned outside the camp.

l: goat for the LORD (sin offering goat), Leviticus, Chapter 16
s: This is the goat on which the lot fell for the LORD, presented and offered as a sin offering for the people. Aaron kills it and brings its blood within the veil, treating it as he did the bull's blood. It is later carried outside the camp and burned.

The scapegoat is the goat on which the lot fell for the scapegoat, presented alive before the LORD to make atonement. Aaron lays both hands on its head and confesses Israel's iniquities over it, and it carries them to a solitary land where it is released in the wilderness. The man who lets it go must wash his clothes and bathe before returning to the camp.

The text sets this day as the tenth day of the seventh month, a statute forever and a Sabbath of solemn rest. The people are to afflict their souls and do no work, native-born and stranger alike, because on this day atonement is made to cleanse them from all their sins before the LORD.

Atonement is made by Aaron for himself and his house, for the Holy Place, the Tent of Meeting, the altar, the priests, and all the people. It is accomplished through blood sprinkling, incense, and the sending away of the live goat, and it is to be done once a year as an everlasting statute, cleansing Israel from all their sins.

The LORD instructs Moses to tell Aaron, his sons, and all the children of Israel that any animal slaughtered for sacrifice, whether in the camp or outside it, must be brought to the door of the Tent of Meeting, where the priest sprinkles the blood on the altar and burns the fat. This is meant to end sacrifices to the goat idols, and anyone who fails to comply is to be cut off from his people. The same requirement applies to strangers living among Israel. The LORD forbids eating blood, explaining that the life of the flesh is in the blood, which he gave on the altar to make atonement. Hunters must pour out the blood of game and cover it with dust, and anyone who eats what died of itself or was torn by animals must wash his clothes and bathe and be unclean until evening, or else bear his iniquity.

The LORD speaks to Moses and commands that all sacrifices be brought to the Tent of Meeting rather than offered in the open field or to the goat idols. He declares he will set his face against anyone who eats blood and cut him off. He explains that he gave the blood on the altar to make atonement because the life of the flesh is in the blood.
Moses receives the LORD's words and is told to relay them to Aaron, his sons, and all the children of Israel. He is the intermediary for the laws on sacrifice, eating blood, and uncleanness.
Aaron, together with his sons, is named as one of the recipients of the LORD's command that Moses is to speak to them. No further action by him is described in this unit.

The children of Israel are commanded to bring any bull, lamb, or goat they kill to the door of the Tent of Meeting, on penalty of being cut off. They must stop sacrificing to the goat idols, must not eat blood, must pour out and cover the blood of hunted game, and must wash and bathe if they eat what died of itself or was torn by animals.

The strangers who live as foreigners among Israel are bound by the same rules: bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices to the Tent of Meeting and not eating blood. They too are to be cut off for eating blood, and a foreigner who eats what died of itself or was torn must wash, bathe, and be unclean until evening.

The door of the Tent of Meeting is the required place to bring offerings to the LORD before his tabernacle. Offering elsewhere brings blood guilt and being cut off. The priest sprinkles the blood on the altar there.
The priest receives the sacrifices brought to the door of the Tent of Meeting as peace offerings. He sprinkles the blood on the LORD's altar and burns the fat as a pleasant aroma to the LORD.
The LORD's altar at the door of the Tent of Meeting is where the priest sprinkles the sacrificial blood. The LORD says he gave the blood on the altar to make atonement for souls.

Blood is declared to hold the life of all flesh, and eating it is forbidden to Israelites and strangers on penalty of being cut off. Sacrificial blood is sprinkled on the altar, and the blood of hunted animals or birds is to be poured out and covered with dust. Killing an animal without bringing it to the Tent of Meeting results in blood being imputed to the man as shed blood.

Sacrifices must be brought to the door of the Tent of Meeting and offered to the LORD as peace offerings through the priest, instead of in the open field or to the goat idols. Failure to do so leads to the offerer being cut off from his people. This is a statute forever throughout their generations.
The LORD says he gave the blood on the altar to make atonement for the people's souls. It is the blood, by reason of the life in it, that makes atonement.

The LORD speaks to Moses and instructs him to tell the children of Israel not to follow the practices of Egypt, where they lived, or Canaan, where they are being brought, but to keep the LORD's statutes and ordinances. The chapter lists forbidden sexual relations, including those with close relatives, a neighbor's wife, a woman during impurity, a man with a man, and animals, and it also forbids giving children to Molech. The LORD explains that the nations being cast out defiled themselves and the land with these acts, so the land vomited out its inhabitants. The Israelites, both native-born and strangers, are warned to avoid these abominations lest the land vomit them out too, and whoever does them will be cut off from their people.

The LORD speaks to Moses, commands the children of Israel to follow his statutes and ordinances rather than the customs of Egypt and Canaan, and repeatedly identifies himself as their God. He forbids a list of sexual relations and child sacrifice to Molech, and says he punished the land's iniquity and is casting out the nations before Israel. He warns that those who commit these abominations will be cut off from their people.

Moses receives the LORD's instruction and is told to speak to the children of Israel, telling them 'I am the LORD your God.' He serves as the intermediary who passes on the commands about conduct and forbidden relations.

The children of Israel are commanded not to act as the people of Egypt, where they lived, or Canaan, where they are being brought, but to keep the LORD's statutes and ordinances. They are given prohibitions on sexual relations and on giving children to Molech, and are warned that doing these abominations will cause the land to vomit them out and lead to being cut off from their people. The commands apply to the native-born and to strangers living among them.

l: nations (those cast out of the land), Leviticus, Chapter 18
s: The nations the LORD is casting out before Israel defiled themselves with these abominations, and the land became defiled. Because of this the LORD punished the land's iniquity and the land vomited out its inhabitants, serving as a warning to Israel.

The land of Canaan is the place the LORD is bringing Israel to, and it was defiled by the abominations of the nations before them. The LORD punished its iniquity and the land vomited out its inhabitants, and it is warned it will do the same to Israel if they defile it.

l: forbidden sexual relations (uncovering nakedness), Leviticus, Chapter 18
s: The chapter forbids uncovering the nakedness of close relatives, including mother, father's wife, sisters, granddaughters, aunts, daughter-in-law, brother's wife, and a woman and her daughter. It also forbids taking a wife in addition to her sister while the sister lives, approaching a woman during impurity, lying with a neighbor's wife, lying with a man as with a woman, and lying with an animal. These are called abominations, defilement, wickedness, and perversion, and those who do them will be cut off from their people.

l: commandments, statutes and ordinances, Leviticus, Chapter 18
s: The LORD commands Israel to do his ordinances and keep his statutes and walk in them, in contrast to the statutes of Egypt and Canaan. A man who does them 'shall live in them.' Keeping them means avoiding the listed abominations and keeping the LORD's requirements.

In Leviticus 19, the LORD tells Moses to speak to the whole congregation of the children of Israel and command them to be holy because the LORD their God is holy. The chapter gives a wide range of commandments: respecting parents, keeping Sabbaths, avoiding idols, rules for eating peace offerings, leaving field and vineyard gleanings for the poor and the foreigner, and prohibitions on stealing, lying, false oaths, oppression, slander, hatred, and vengeance. It commands loving one's neighbor as oneself and loving the stranger as oneself, since Israel lived as foreigners in Egypt. It also covers rules on mixed kinds, a trespass offering for a case involving a slave girl, fruit trees, blood, sorcery, mourning and bodily practices, mediums, honoring the elderly, and just weights and measures. It closes with a charge to observe all the LORD's statutes and ordinances.

The LORD speaks to Moses and instructs him to tell Israel to be holy because he is holy. He repeatedly identifies himself as the LORD their God, who brought them out of Egypt, and grounds a wide set of commandments in that identity.
Moses receives the LORD's word and is told to speak it to all the congregation of the children of Israel. He serves as the intermediary who passes on the commandments of this chapter.

The whole congregation of the children of Israel is commanded to be holy as the LORD is holy. They receive laws on worship, sacrifice, justice, care for the poor, treatment of neighbors and strangers, and are told to observe all his statutes and ordinances.

The chapter sets out the commandments that express holiness: respecting parents, keeping Sabbaths, avoiding idols, honest dealing, justice without partiality, and loving one's neighbor. It also includes rules on offerings, harvest, fruit trees, blood, sorcery, mediums, bodily practices, and just weights and measures, all ending with a call to observe every statute and ordinance.

The stranger living as a foreigner in the land must not be wronged. He is to be treated as the native-born and loved as oneself, because Israel was once a foreigner in Egypt; gleanings of field and vineyard are also left for the foreigner.
Neighbors are not to be oppressed, robbed, slandered, hated, endangered, or taken vengeance on. They are to be judged in righteousness, rebuked when necessary, and loved as oneself.

In Leviticus 20 the LORD instructs Moses to tell the children of Israel the penalties for serious offenses. He prescribes death by stoning for giving offspring to Molech, for cursing parents, and for being a medium or wizard, and he declares he will set his face against those who turn to mediums and wizards. He lists death or being cut off as penalties for adultery, for various forbidden sexual relations such as incest, same-sex intercourse, and bestiality, and for lying with a woman during her period. He calls the people to sanctify themselves and be holy, to keep his statutes so the land does not vomit them out, and not to follow the customs of the nation he is casting out. He reminds them he has separated them from the peoples and promised them a land flowing with milk and honey.

The LORD speaks to Moses and gives the children of Israel laws with penalties, declaring he will set his face against and cut off those who give offspring to Molech or turn to mediums and wizards. He identifies himself as the one who sanctifies Israel, who is holy, and who has separated them from the peoples to be his. He is casting out the nation before Israel and will give them its land.

The children of Israel, along with the strangers living among them, are told the penalties for idolatry, cursing parents, adultery, and forbidden sexual relations. They are commanded to sanctify themselves, keep the LORD's statutes and ordinances, distinguish clean from unclean animals, and not walk in the customs of the nation being cast out. They are told they will inherit that land and have been set apart to be the LORD's.

Molech is the recipient of offspring given by anyone among the children of Israel or the strangers living in Israel. Those who play the prostitute after Molech are to be put to death or cut off from their people.

l: child sacrifice to Molech, Leviticus, Chapter 20
s: Giving any of one's offspring to Molech is punishable by death, with the people of the land to stone the offender. The LORD says it defiles his sanctuary and profanes his holy name, and he will cut off the person. If the people hide their eyes and do not execute the offender, he will cut off the man, his family, and all who follow him.

l: people of the land, Leviticus, Chapter 20
s: The people of the land are commanded to stone anyone who gives offspring to Molech. The LORD warns that if they all hide their eyes and do not put the offender to death, he will set his face against the man and his family and cut them off.

Anyone who turns to mediums and wizards is described as playing the prostitute after them, and the LORD will set his face against that person and cut him off from his people. A man or woman who is a medium or wizard is to be put to death by stoning, with their blood upon themselves.
Adultery with another man's wife, or a neighbor's wife, is punished by the death of both the adulterer and the adulteress.

l: forbidden sexual relations (uncovering nakedness), Leviticus, Chapter 20
s: A long list of forbidden unions is given, including with a father's wife, a daughter-in-law, a male, a wife and her mother, an animal, a sister, a woman during her period, an aunt, an uncle's wife, and a brother's wife. Penalties include death, burning with fire, being cut off, or dying childless, and the texts calls these acts uncovering nakedness, perversion, abomination, wickedness, or impurity.

l: nation being cast out, Leviticus, Chapter 20
s: The LORD is casting this nation out before Israel because they did all the forbidden things, and he abhorred them. Israel is told not to walk in its customs.

l: land (land given to Israel), Leviticus, Chapter 20
s: The LORD says Israel will inherit and possess the land of the nation he is casting out, a land flowing with milk and honey. Israel is warned that if they do not keep his statutes and ordinances, the land may vomit them out.

The LORD commands the people to sanctify themselves and be holy because he is the LORD their God and is holy. He has set them apart from the peoples to be his, and they are to keep his statutes and distinguish clean from unclean animals, birds, and creatures that teem on the ground.

In Leviticus 21 the LORD instructs Moses to speak to Aaron and the priests, the sons of Aaron, about the holiness required of them. Ordinary priests may not defile themselves for the dead except for near relatives, may not shave their heads or beards or cut their flesh, and may not marry a prostitute, a profane woman, or a divorced woman. A priest's daughter who plays the prostitute is to be burned with fire. The high priest, anointed with oil, is held to stricter rules: he may not go near any dead body, even for his father or mother, may not leave the sanctuary, and may marry only a virgin of his own people. Any descendant of Aaron with a defect, such as blindness, lameness, deformity, or damaged testicles, may not approach the altar or veil to offer the bread of God, though he may eat of the holy and most holy food; Moses then relays all this to Aaron, his sons, and all Israel.

The LORD speaks to Moses and gives rules for priestly holiness, declaring that he sanctifies the priests and the sanctuaries and is himself holy. He commands that the priests be holy because they offer his offerings made by fire, the bread of their God.
Moses receives the LORD's words and is told to speak to the priests and to Aaron. At the end he relays these instructions to Aaron, his sons, and all the children of Israel.

Aaron is addressed as the ancestor of the priestly line, and the LORD tells Moses to say that none of his offspring with a defect may approach to offer the bread of God. Moses then speaks these rules to Aaron and his sons.

The priests are commanded to be holy to their God and not profane his name. They may not defile themselves for the dead except near relatives, may not shave their heads or beards or cut their flesh, and may not marry a prostitute, a profane woman, or a divorced woman. A priest's daughter who profanes herself by prostitution profanes her father and is to be burned with fire.

The high priest, whose head is anointed with oil and who is consecrated to wear the garments, may not let his hair hang loose or tear his clothes. He may not go in to any dead body, even for his father or mother, and may not leave the sanctuary. He must marry a virgin of his own people, not a widow, a divorced woman, a defiled woman, or a prostitute, so that he does not profane his offspring.

l: mourning and contact with the dead, Leviticus, Chapter 21
s: A priest may not defile himself for the dead among his people, except for his mother, father, son, daughter, brother, and his unmarried virgin sister who is near to him. The high priest is forbidden even this and may not defile himself for his father or mother. Priests also may not shave their heads, shave the corners of their beards, or cut their flesh.

l: marriage restrictions for priests, Leviticus, Chapter 21
s: A priest may not marry a prostitute, a profane woman, or a woman divorced from her husband, because he is holy to his God. The high priest must take a virgin of his own people as wife and may not marry a widow, a divorced woman, a defiled woman, or a prostitute, lest he profane his offspring.

l: physical defects disqualifying priests, Leviticus, Chapter 21
s: No descendant of Aaron who has a defect may approach to offer the offerings or the bread of God. The listed defects include blindness, lameness, a flat nose, any deformity, an injured foot or hand, being hunchbacked or a dwarf, a defect in the eye, an itching disease, scabs, or damaged testicles. Such a man may still eat the most holy and the holy food, but may not come near the veil or the altar, so that he does not profane the sanctuaries.

l: offerings and bread of God, Leviticus, Chapter 21
s: The priests offer the LORD's offerings made by fire, called the bread of their God, which is the reason they must be holy. Only priests without defects may draw near to offer it, though a defective priest may eat of both the most holy and the holy portions.

In Leviticus 22 the LORD instructs Moses to tell Aaron and his sons how to handle the holy things of the children of Israel without profaning his name. Priests who are unclean through leprosy, a discharge, or contact with the dead or other uncleanness may not eat the holy things until they are clean and have bathed. The chapter also specifies who in a priest's household may eat the holy things, and requires a fifth part added as restitution for unwitting eating. The LORD then sets rules for offerings: animals must be male and without defect, young animals stay seven days with their mothers, a mother and its young are not killed on the same day, and a thanksgiving sacrifice must be eaten the same day. The chapter closes with a call to keep the commandments, since the LORD sanctifies Israel and brought them out of Egypt.

The LORD speaks to Moses three times, giving rules on priestly purity, eating the holy things, and acceptable offerings. He declares that he sanctifies the priests and the people, and identifies himself as the one who brought Israel out of Egypt to be their God.

Moses receives three separate messages from the LORD and is told to relay them to Aaron, his sons, and all the children of Israel. He acts as the intermediary for the instructions on holiness and offerings.

Aaron is to be told, with his sons, to separate themselves from the holy things so as not to profane the LORD's name. He is also addressed, with his sons and all Israel, regarding offerings that must be without defect.

Aaron's sons, as priests, must keep away from the holy things while unclean and may eat them only after being clean and bathing. They are warned that profaning the holy things brings sin and death, and they are told not to cause the people's holy things to bear guilt.

The children of Israel make the holy things holy to the LORD, and they and the foreigners among them are told to bring offerings that are acceptable. A person who eats a holy thing unwittingly must add a fifth of its value and give it to the priest. They are urged to keep the LORD's commandments and not profane his name.

l: holy things of the LORD, Leviticus, Chapter 22
s: The holy things are the offerings the children of Israel make holy to the LORD, and priests eat them as their bread. A priest may eat them only when clean, and only members of his household, such as purchased slaves, those born in his house, and a widowed or divorced childless daughter, may share. Strangers, foreigners living with the priests, hired servants, and a daughter married to an outsider may not eat them.

Uncleanness comes from leprosy, a discharge, touching the dead, a seminal emission, or a creeping thing. An unclean person who approaches the holy things is cut off from the LORD. Contact makes a person unclean until evening, and the person must bathe before eating the holy things, after sundown.

Burnt offerings, peace offerings, vows, free will offerings, and thanksgiving sacrifices must be offered so that the giver is accepted. Young animals are acceptable from the eighth day, a cow or ewe and its young are not killed on the same day, and a thanksgiving sacrifice must be eaten the same day with nothing left until morning.

Offerings of bulls, sheep, or goats must be males without defect to be accepted. Animals that are blind, injured, maimed, warty, festering, running with sores, or with bruised, crushed, broken, or cut testicles may not be offered. An animal with a deformity may be given as a free will offering but not accepted for a vow, and defective animals from a foreigner's hand are also not accepted.

In Leviticus 23 the LORD instructs Moses to tell the children of Israel about his set feasts, which are to be proclaimed as holy convocations. The chapter begins with the weekly Sabbath, then lists the Passover and feast of unleavened bread in the first month, the first fruits sheaf offering, and the fifty-day count to a new meal offering with two loaves. It continues with the instruction to leave the field corners and gleanings for the poor and the foreigner, then the day of trumpets, the day of atonement, and the feast of booths in the seventh month. The chapter ends with a statement that Moses declared the appointed feasts to the children of Israel.

The LORD speaks to Moses in several separate messages, giving instructions for the set feasts and claiming them as his own. He requires offerings made by fire, warns that anyone who does work on the day of atonement or does not deny himself will be cut off or destroyed from among his people, and identifies himself as the God who brought Israel out of Egypt.

Moses receives the LORD's words and is told to speak them to the children of Israel on each feast. The unit closes by stating that Moses declared the appointed feasts of the LORD to the children of Israel.

The children of Israel are the people commanded to proclaim the feasts as holy convocations, to rest from regular work on them, and to bring the prescribed offerings. They are told to observe the feasts as statutes forever, to leave field corners and gleanings for the poor and foreigner, and to dwell in temporary shelters so that their generations remember the exodus from Egypt.

l: set feasts of the LORD, Leviticus, Chapter 23
s: The set feasts are defined as the LORD's own appointed times, to be proclaimed as holy convocations in their appointed season. The unit lists them in order: the Sabbath, Passover, unleavened bread, the first fruits and the fifty-day feast, trumpets, atonement, and booths. Each is to be kept with its own offerings in addition to the Sabbaths, gifts, vows, and free will offerings.

The Sabbath is set out first: work is done six days, and the seventh is a Sabbath of solemn rest and a holy convocation with no work, kept in all their dwellings. It also serves as a reference point for dating the wave sheaf, which is offered on the day after the Sabbath, and for counting seven Sabbaths. The day of atonement is itself called a Sabbath of solemn rest.
The LORD's Passover is set on the fourteenth day of the first month, in the evening.

l: feast of unleavened bread, Leviticus, Chapter 23
s: The feast of unleavened bread begins on the fifteenth day of the first month and lasts seven days, during which unleavened bread is eaten. The first and seventh days are holy convocations with no regular work, and an offering made by fire is brought to the LORD on each of the seven days.

l: offering of the first fruits sheaf, Leviticus, Chapter 23
s: After entering the land and reaping its harvest, the people are to bring a sheaf of the first fruits to the priest, who waves it before the LORD on the day after the Sabbath. On that day a male lamb a year old without defect is offered as a burnt offering, with a meal offering of two tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil and a drink offering of a fourth of a hin of wine. No bread, roasted grain, or fresh grain may be eaten until this offering is brought, as a statute forever.

l: feast of weeks (Pentecost, fifty days after the sheaf), Leviticus, Chapter 23
s: The feast is dated by counting seven completed Sabbaths from the wave sheaf, then fifty days to a new meal offering. The people bring two loaves baked with yeast from two tenths of an ephah of fine flour as a wave offering of first fruits. With them they offer seven lambs, one young bull, and two rams as burnt offerings, one male goat as a sin offering, and two male lambs as peace offerings. The day is a holy convocation with no regular work, a statute forever.

l: day of trumpets (first day of seventh month), Leviticus, Chapter 23
s: The first day of the seventh month is a solemn rest and a memorial of blowing of trumpets, a holy convocation. No regular work is to be done, and an offering made by fire is brought to the LORD.

The tenth day of the seventh month is the day of atonement, a holy convocation to make atonement for the people before the LORD. The people must afflict or deny themselves, do no kind of work, and offer an offering made by fire. Whoever does not deny himself is cut off from his people, and whoever works is destroyed by the LORD. It is a Sabbath of solemn rest kept from evening to evening, a statute forever.

The feast of booths begins on the fifteenth day of the seventh month and lasts seven days, with a holy convocation on the first day and a solemn assembly on the eighth, each with no regular work. The people take the fruit of majestic trees, palm branches, boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook, and rejoice before the LORD seven days. All native-born Israelites dwell in temporary shelters so their generations will know the LORD had Israel dwell in such shelters when he brought them out of Egypt.

The feasts call for offerings made by fire, including burnt offerings, meal offerings, sacrifices, and drink offerings, each on its own day. The unit specifies animals and flour amounts for the first fruits and the fifty-day feast. It states that these are in addition to the Sabbaths, gifts, vows, and free will offerings given to the LORD.

The LORD instructs Moses to have the children of Israel bring pure olive oil so a lamp burns continually, with Aaron tending the lamps from evening to morning. He also commands that twelve cakes of fine flour be set in two rows of six on the pure gold table with frankincense, renewed every Sabbath, and eaten by Aaron and his sons in a holy place. The son of an Israelite woman, Shelomith of the tribe of Dan, and an Egyptian father blasphemes the Name and curses during a quarrel in the camp, and he is held in custody until the LORD's will is declared. The LORD orders that he be stoned by the congregation and sets out laws: death for blasphemy, death for killing a man, restitution for killing an animal, and equal retribution for injuries, with one law for foreigner and native-born. Moses relays this, and the children of Israel stone the man outside the camp as commanded.

The LORD speaks to Moses about the continual lamp oil and the twelve cakes of bread, then declares his will on the blasphemer after the man is held in custody. He commands stoning for the blasphemer, sets out laws on killing and injury, and declares one law for the foreigner and the native-born.

Moses receives the LORD's instructions on the lamp and the bread, and the people bring the blasphemer to him. He waits for the LORD's will, then speaks the commands to the children of Israel, who carry out the stoning.

Aaron is to keep the lamps in order outside the veil of the Testimony in the Tent of Meeting from evening to morning continually. He and his sons are to eat the bread of the offerings in a holy place, as it is most holy to him.

The children of Israel are commanded to bring pure olive oil for the lamp, and the bread is an everlasting covenant on their behalf. They hold the blasphemer in custody, and those who heard him lay hands on his head, and the congregation stones him as the LORD commanded.

l: son of the Israelite woman, Leviticus, Chapter 24
s: He is the son of Shelomith, daughter of Dibri of the tribe of Dan, and of an Egyptian father. He strives with a man of Israel in the camp, blasphemes the Name and curses, is put in custody, and is then taken outside the camp and stoned to death.

l: blasphemy of the Name, Leviticus, Chapter 24
s: The son of the Israelite woman blasphemes the Name and curses during a quarrel. The LORD declares that whoever blasphemes his name shall surely be put to death by stoning by all the congregation, foreigner and native-born alike.

l: stoning of the blasphemer, Leviticus, Chapter 24
s: The LORD orders that the one who cursed be brought out of the camp, that those who heard him lay their hands on his head, and that all the congregation stone him. The children of Israel do so, as the LORD commanded Moses.

The LORD states that one who strikes a man mortally shall be put to death and one who kills an animal shall make it good, life for life. An injurer is to suffer what he has done: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, under one law for foreigner and native-born.

On Mount Sinai the LORD instructs Moses to tell the children of Israel the rules for the land they will enter. Every seventh year is a Sabbath of rest for the land, and after seven cycles of seven years the fiftieth year is a Jubilee, announced by trumpet on the Day of Atonement, in which liberty is proclaimed and people return to their property and family. The chapter regulates fair sales based on years of crops, forbids permanent sale of the land because it belongs to the LORD, and sets out redemption rights through kinsmen, with special rules for houses in walled cities and Levite cities. It also commands support of a poor brother without interest, forbids making him a slave, and provides for his redemption or release at Jubilee, while allowing slaves to be bought from surrounding nations.

The LORD speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai and gives the laws of the Sabbath year and Jubilee. He declares that the land is his and that the Israelites are strangers and his servants whom he brought out of Egypt. He promises a blessing in the sixth year that will yield enough fruit for three years.

The children of Israel are told that when they enter the land they must keep the Sabbath year, count the Jubilee, deal fairly in sales, and not wrong one another. They are commanded to redeem relatives' property, to lend to a poor brother without interest, and not to rule over fellow Israelites harshly. They are called the LORD's servants, so they may not be sold as slaves.

The seventh year is a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land, in which fields are not sown, vineyards are not pruned, and what grows by itself is not reaped. Its produce serves as food for the people, servants, strangers, livestock and animals. The LORD promises that the sixth year's blessing will provide for the seventh.

The fiftieth year, following seven Sabbaths of years (forty-nine years), is made holy by a trumpet blast on the Day of Atonement. Liberty is proclaimed, and each person returns to his property and family, with no sowing or reaping. Prices of land are set by the number of years remaining until it, and sold land and indentured Israelites are released in it.

l: land (land given to Israel), Leviticus, Chapter 25
s: The land is to keep a Sabbath to the LORD and is not to be sold in perpetuity, because it is the LORD's. Its fruit will be abundant and the people will dwell in safety if they keep his statutes. Houses in walled cities are an exception to release, while village houses are treated as fields and Levite pasture lands may never be sold.

A poor brother who sells part of his possessions may have them redeemed by his nearest kinsman, or he may redeem them himself if he prospers. He is to be upheld, given no loans at interest or food for profit, and treated as a hired servant rather than a slave. He and his children go free at the Jubilee, and if sold to a foreigner he may be redeemed by relatives or himself at a price based on the years remaining.

The land redemption law requires that a redemption be granted in all the land of their possession. A kinsman may buy back sold property, or the seller may reckon the years since the sale and repay the surplus, otherwise it is released at the Jubilee. A house in a walled city can be redeemed only within one full year, while Levites may redeem their city houses at any time.

Chapter 26 closes the Sinai laws with a covenant of blessings and curses addressed by the LORD to the Israelites through Moses. After forbidding idols and requiring Sabbath-keeping, the LORD promises rain, abundant harvests, peace, victory over enemies, fruitfulness, and his own presence if the people obey his statutes and commandments. If they refuse, he threatens escalating punishments in stages of sevenfold intensity: terror, disease, drought, wild animals, sword, pestilence, famine, cannibalism, ruined cities, and scattering among the nations. The land will then enjoy its Sabbaths while desolate, and the survivors will waste away in fear in enemy lands. Yet if they confess their iniquity and humble their hearts, the LORD promises to remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham and not utterly reject them.

The LORD forbids idols, demands Sabbath-keeping, and promises to walk among the Israelites as their God if they obey. He pledges to punish disobedience in escalating stages of sevenfold severity, yet to remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham and not destroy them utterly if they confess and humble themselves. He identifies himself as the one who brought them out of Egypt and broke the bars of their yoke.

The Israelites are told that their obedience will bring blessing and their rejection of the LORD's laws will bring severe punishment. If disobedient, they will be defeated, scattered among the nations, and left fearful in enemy lands. If they confess their own and their fathers' iniquity and humble their uncircumcised hearts, the LORD will remember his covenant and not reject them.

The LORD promises to establish his covenant with the obedient, while those who reject his statutes and break the covenant face vengeance of the covenant through the sword. Even in exile, the LORD will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham and the covenant with their ancestors whom he brought out of Egypt. He will not break it by destroying them utterly.

The Israelites are commanded to keep the LORD's Sabbaths. The land will enjoy its Sabbaths while lying desolate and the people are in enemy lands, receiving the rest it did not have while they lived on it.

The land yields increase, fruit, and safety under obedience, but under disobedience becomes like iron and bronze, unproductive, and finally desolate. Its cities are laid waste and its enemies who settle there are astonished. It will rest and enjoy its Sabbaths during the exile, and the LORD promises to remember it.

In the blessings, the Israelites chase their enemies, who fall before them by the sword. In the curses, enemies eat the people's seed, rule over them, receive them into their hands, and dwell in the desolated land. The scattered survivors live in the enemies' lands, where they flee in terror and perish.

Obedience brings rains in season, abundant crops and fruit, safe dwelling, peace, removal of evil animals, and victory over enemies, with five chasing a hundred. The LORD also promises fruitfulness, multiplication, a confirmed covenant, his tent among them, and his walking among them as their God.

Disobedience brings punishments in four escalating stages, each sevenfold: terror, consumption, fever, defeat, drought, wild animals, sword, pestilence, famine, and cannibalism. They culminate in destroyed high places, ruined cities and sanctuaries, scattering among the nations, and faintness of heart in exile. These punishments are not final, since confession and humility lead the LORD to remember his covenant.
