In Leviticus 27 the LORD instructs Moses to tell the children of Israel how to value and redeem things dedicated to Him. Persons consecrated by vow are valued in shekels of silver by age and sex, with the priest adjusting the value for the poor. Dedicated animals, houses, and fields are valued by the priest, and redeeming them requires adding a fifth, with fields adjusted according to the years remaining to the Year of Jubilee. Permanently devoted things cannot be sold or redeemed, firstborn animals already belong to the LORD, and the tithe of the land and of herds and flocks is holy to the LORD. The chapter closes by stating that these are the commandments given to Moses on Mount Sinai.
The LORD speaks to Moses and gives regulations for vows, valuations, and dedicated things. He claims firstborn animals, permanently devoted things, and the tithe as holy to Himself.
Moses receives the LORD's instructions and is told to relay them to the children of Israel. The chapter ends by noting these commandments were given to him on Mount Sinai.

The Year of Jubilee determines the value of dedicated fields, with the valuation reduced according to the years remaining after it. A bought field dedicated to the LORD returns in the Jubilee to its original owner, while an unredeemed or sold field becomes holy and owned by the priests.

The priest assesses the value of the poor person's vow, unclean animals, houses, and fields, and his evaluation stands. He reckons the reduced value of fields by the years remaining to the Jubilee, and fields not redeemed come to be owned by the priests.

l: vow of consecrating persons and valuation, Leviticus, Chapter 27
s: A person consecrated by vow is valued in shekels of silver of the sanctuary by age and sex: for a male aged twenty to sixty, fifty shekels, and thirty for a female. Younger and older people have lower values, and a person too poor to pay is set before the priest, who assigns a value according to his ability to pay.

l: animals dedicated to the LORD, Leviticus, Chapter 27
s: Animals of a kind offered to the LORD become holy when given, and may not be altered or exchanged, since an exchanged animal and its substitute both become holy. Unclean animals are valued by the priest and may be redeemed with a fifth added, and firstborn animals cannot be dedicated because they are already the LORD's.
A man who dedicates his house has it evaluated by the priest, and that evaluation stands. If he redeems it, he adds a fifth of the valuation money and it remains his.

A dedicated field of one's possession is valued by seed, with a homer of barley sowing valued at fifty shekels of silver, and the value is reduced for years after the Jubilee. If it is not redeemed or has been sold, it becomes holy to the LORD at the Jubilee and is owned by the priests, while a bought field returns to its original owner.

Redeeming an unclean animal, a house, a field, or part of the tithe requires paying the valuation plus a fifth part. Redeeming is not allowed for permanently devoted things, and a field that is not redeemed or has been sold cannot be redeemed anymore.

Anything permanently devoted to the LORD, whether man, animal, or field, cannot be sold or redeemed and is most holy to the LORD. A person devoted to destruction cannot be ransomed and must be put to death.

The tithe of the land's seed and tree fruit is the LORD's and holy, and redeeming any of it requires adding a fifth. The tenth of herds and flocks passing under the rod is holy, with no examining for good or bad and no exchange, and it cannot be redeemed.

l: The Book of Ruth, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 1
s: During a famine in the days of the judges, Elimelech took his wife Naomi and their two sons, Mahlon and Chilion, from Bethlehem Judah to Moab. Elimelech died, the sons married Orpah and Ruth, and after about ten years both sons died, leaving Naomi bereaved. Hearing that the LORD had given his people bread, Naomi set out to return to Judah and urged her daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers' houses. Orpah kissed her and went back, but Ruth clung to Naomi and vowed that Naomi's people and God would be hers. The two arrived in Bethlehem at the start of barley harvest, where Naomi asked to be called Mara because of the bitterness the Almighty had brought her.

l: Naomi, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 1
s: Naomi moved to Moab with her husband Elimelech and two sons, and was left bereaved when all three died. She returned to Bethlehem after hearing the LORD had provided bread, urging her daughters-in-law to turn back. Upon arrival she asked to be called Mara, saying she went out full and came home empty.

l: Ruth, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 1
s: Ruth, a Moabite, married one of Naomi's sons and lived in Moab about ten years. She refused to leave Naomi, vowing that Naomi's people would be her people and Naomi's God her God, and that only death would part them. She came with Naomi to Bethlehem at the beginning of barley harvest.

l: Orpah, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 1
s: Orpah, a Moabite woman, married one of Naomi's sons. After weeping, she kissed her mother-in-law Naomi and went back to her people and her god, while Ruth stayed.

l: LORD, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 1
s: The LORD is said to have visited his people in giving them bread, which prompted Naomi's return. Naomi invokes him to deal kindly with her daughters-in-law and grant them rest, and she attributes her losses to his hand going out against her, saying he testified against her and brought her home empty. Ruth swears by him in her vow.

l: Moab, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 1
s: Moab is the country where Naomi's family went to live during the famine, and where Elimelech, Mahlon and Chilion died. Orpah and Ruth were Moabite women who married the sons there. Naomi left it after hearing that the LORD had given bread to his people.

l: Bethlehem, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 1
s: Bethlehem Judah is the home of Elimelech's family, who left it during a famine. When Naomi and Ruth arrived at the beginning of barley harvest, the whole city was excited and asked whether this was Naomi.

l: The Book of Ruth, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 2
s: Ruth the Moabitess goes to glean in the fields and happens upon the portion belonging to Boaz, a wealthy relative of Naomi's husband from the family of Elimelech. Boaz learns who she is, praises her loyalty to her mother-in-law, tells her to stay close to his maidens, and orders his young men not to touch or rebuke her. He feeds her at mealtime and instructs his workers to pull out extra grain for her. Ruth gleans until evening, gathers about an ephah of barley, and brings it and leftover food to Naomi. Naomi blesses Boaz, identifies him as a near kinsman, and Ruth stays with Boaz's maidens through the barley and wheat harvests while living with Naomi.

l: Ruth, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 2
s: Ruth asks Naomi's leave to glean, goes to the field, and happens upon Boaz's portion. She bows before Boaz in gratitude, is praised for leaving her homeland to care for Naomi, eats with the reapers, and gleans about an ephah of barley. She brings it home to Naomi, stays close to Boaz's maidens through the barley and wheat harvests, and lives with Naomi.

l: Naomi, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 2
s: Naomi lets Ruth go to glean, and receives the barley and the leftover food Ruth brings back. On hearing Boaz's name she blesses him and says he is a close relative, one of their near kinsmen. She approves of Ruth staying with his maidens so she will not be harmed in another field.

l: Boaz, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 2
s: Boaz is introduced as a mighty man of wealth and a relative of Naomi's husband, of the family of Elimelech. He greets his reapers with a blessing, asks about Ruth, and tells her to stay in his field and drink from the vessels, saying he has commanded the young men not to touch her. He praises her kindness to Naomi, invites her to eat, and orders his men to let her glean among the sheaves and to leave extra grain for her.

l: reapers (Boaz's reapers), The Book of Ruth, Chapter 2
s: The reapers answer Boaz's greeting by blessing him in return, and the servant set over them reports that Ruth has gleaned since morning, resting only briefly. At mealtime they pass Ruth parched grain as she sits beside them. Boaz's young men are commanded not to touch, reproach, or rebuke her, and to pull out some grain from the bundles for her.

l: field (Boaz's field), The Book of Ruth, Chapter 2
s: Ruth happens to come to the portion of the field belonging to Boaz, who is of Elimelech's family. Boaz tells her to glean only there and stay close to his maidens, and it is the place where she works until evening. She remains in his field through the end of the barley and wheat harvests.

l: gleaning (Ruth's gleaning), The Book of Ruth, Chapter 2
s: Ruth proposes to glean among the ears of grain after someone who will show her favor, and begins after the reapers. Boaz extends it by letting her glean even among the sheaves and having extra grain pulled out for her. She gleans until evening, beats out about an ephah of barley, and continues through the barley and wheat harvests.

l: The Book of Ruth, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 3
s: Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, tells Ruth to wash, anoint herself, dress, and go to the threshing floor where their kinsman Boaz will be winnowing barley, then to lie at his feet once he has eaten and drunk. Ruth does all that Naomi says, and at midnight Boaz is startled to find her there; she identifies herself and asks him to spread his garment over her because he is a near kinsman. Boaz blesses her, tells her not to be afraid, and says the city knows she is a worthy woman, but he explains that a kinsman nearer than he exists. He promises that if that kinsman will not perform the kinsman's duty, he himself will, and he lets her stay until morning, then sends her away before she can be recognized, giving her six measures of barley. Ruth returns to Naomi and reports everything, and Naomi tells her to wait, since Boaz will not rest until he has settled the matter that day.

l: Naomi, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 3
s: Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, proposes seeking rest for Ruth and gives detailed instructions: wash, anoint, dress, go to Boaz at the threshing floor, and uncover his feet and lie down after he has eaten and drunk. When Ruth returns, Naomi asks how it went and hears everything. She tells Ruth to wait, because Boaz will not rest until he has settled the matter that day.

l: Ruth, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 3
s: Ruth agrees to do all Naomi says and goes down to the threshing floor, where she uncovers Boaz's feet and lies down. At midnight she identifies herself as his servant and asks him to spread his garment over her because he is a near kinsman. Boaz praises her kindness and worth, she stays until morning and leaves before she can be recognized, carrying six measures of barley. She reports everything to Naomi.

l: Boaz, The Book of Ruth, Chapter 3
s: Boaz is described by Naomi as a kinsman who will be winnowing barley that night. After eating and drinking he lies down at the end of the heap of grain, wakes startled at midnight, and finds Ruth. He blesses her, praises her kindness and reputation as a worthy woman, and says a nearer kinsman exists. He swears by the LORD to do the kinsman's duty if the other will not, asks that her visit be kept secret, gives her six measures of barley, and goes into the city.

l: near kinsman (of Boaz and Elimelech's family), The Book of Ruth, Chapter 3
s: Boaz reveals that there is a kinsman nearer than he is. This man is to be given the chance in the morning to perform the kinsman's duty for Ruth. If he will not, Boaz will do it.
